## The Circle Estimator

We begin with a classic Monte Carlo application. Inscribe a circle in a square, scatter points uniformly over the square, and count how many land inside the circle. That fraction, times 4, estimates $\pi$.

```{ojs}

// This page uses VM.sampling.seededRandom, VM.plotting.persistentPlot, VM.ui.statRow,

VM = window.VM
```

Let $(X, Y)$ be uniformly distributed on $[-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]$ and define the indicator random variable
$$I(X, Y) = \mathbf{1}_{\{X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1\}} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1 \text{ (inside circle)} \\
0 & \text{if } X^2 + Y^2 > 1 \text{ (outside circle)}
\end{cases}$$

The point $(X, Y)$ lands in the circle with probability equal to the ratio of the two areas, $P(X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1) = \pi/4$, so $I \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi/4)$ and $\pi = 4\mathbb{E}[I]$. By linearity of expectation, the average of $4I$ over $N$ samples therefore has mean $\pi$, whether or not the samples are independent.

::: {#def-circle-estimator}
## The Circle Estimator
Given $N$ independent samples $(X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_N, Y_N)$, write $I_i = I(X_i, Y_i)$ and estimate $\pi$ by
$$\hat{\pi}_N = \frac{4}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i = \frac{4 \cdot \text{(number of points inside the circle)}}{N}.$$
:::

We'll next answer the question: Is this a good estimator? 

## Convergence Analysis

Start with a simulation. *Running estimates* follows 8 independent runs as points are added one at a time. *Error decay* repeats the experiment 200 times and measures the typical error at each $N$.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
piRunsPlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "400px"})
piErrorPlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "400px"})

// Log-spaced sample sizes up to 10,000, so the runs read evenly on a log axis.
piRunCounts = checkpoints(10000, 24)
piRuns = runningCircleEstimates(VM.sampling.seededRandom(42), piRunCounts, 8)
piErrors = randomCircleErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(43), checkpoints(10000), 200)

// A key to go under a half-width chart, where mathviz hides its overlay legend.
function piLegendKey(rows) {
  const key = document.createElement("div")
  key.className = "pi-legend-key"
  for (const row of rows) {
    const item = document.createElement("div")
    const swatch = document.createElement("span")
    swatch.className = "pi-legend-swatch"
    if (row.dashed) {
      swatch.classList.add("pi-legend-swatch-dashed")
      swatch.style.borderColor = row.color
    } else {
      swatch.style.background = row.color
    }
    const text = document.createElement("span")
    text.textContent = row.label
    item.append(swatch, text)
    key.append(item)
  }
  return key
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const xs = [], rms = [], lo = [], hi = [], reference = []
  const last = piErrors[piErrors.length - 1]
  for (const p of piErrors) {
    xs.push(p.n)
    rms.push(p.error)
    lo.push(p.lo)
    hi.push(p.hi)
    // Slope -1/2 on log-log axes, raised above the band so the two can be compared.
    reference.push(2.5 * last.error * Math.sqrt(last.n / p.n))
  }
  // Unnamed traces: the key below stands in for the legend.
  const chart = VM.plotting.plotWithLegend(piErrorPlot, [
    {x: xs, y: rms, type: "scatter", mode: "lines+markers", hoverinfo: "skip",
      line: {color: chartColors.fn, width: 2}, marker: {color: chartColors.fn, size: 4}},
    // The 10%-90% band: the upper edge, then the lower edge filled up to it.
    {x: xs, y: hi, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", hoverinfo: "skip", line: {width: 0, color: chartColors.fn}},
    {x: xs, y: lo, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", hoverinfo: "skip", line: {width: 0, color: chartColors.fn},
      fill: "tonexty", fillcolor: VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.15)},
    {x: xs, y: reference, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", hoverinfo: "skip",
      line: {color: chartColors.ink, dash: "dash", width: 1.5}}
  ], {
    title: {text: "Error decay"}, margin: {t: 40},
    xaxis: {title: "Sample size (N)", type: "log"}, yaxis: {title: "|estimate − π|", type: "log", exponentformat: "power"},
    hovermode: false, uirevision: "static", autosize: true
  })

  const figure = document.createElement("div")
  figure.append(chart, piLegendKey([
    {label: "RMS error", color: chartColors.fn},
    {label: "Middle 80% of runs", color: VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.15)},
    {label: "Slope −1/2", color: chartColors.ink, dashed: true}
  ]))
  return figure
}
```

:::

Running estimates from 8 runs, and the error over 200 runs.

::::

As $N$ increases, the runs close in on $\pi$ and the spread between them shrinks. On log-log axes the error falls along a line parallel to the reference, so it decays like $N^{-1/2}$. The exercises below ask you to derive this rate and explain what you see.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Monte Carlo Principle
This example demonstrates the fundamental Monte Carlo approach: reformulate a deterministic problem (computing $\pi$) as the expectation of a random variable, then estimate that expectation using sample averages.
:::

## Buffon's Needle

A second, much older way to estimate $\pi$ by random sampling goes back to Buffon (1777). Rule the plane with parallel lines a distance $t$ apart, drop needles of length $\ell \le t$ on it at random, and count how many cross a line. Surprisingly, this count can be used to estimate $\pi$.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
buffonMaxN = 10000
buffonDefaultSeed = 1
buffonDefaultN = 100
buffonDefaultLength = 0.8
buffonShapeOptions = ["Needle", "Noodle"]
// Lines y = 0, 1, ..., 6 (spacing t = 1) across a board 8 wide.
buffonSpacing = 1
buffonWidth = 8
buffonHeight = 6

buffonTraceOptions = ["Crossing a line", "Not crossing", "Lines"]
buffonTraceColors = new Map([
  ["Crossing a line", chartColors.alt],
  ["Not crossing", chartColors.fn],
  ["Lines", chartColors.muted]
])
```

```{ojs}
}
```

```{ojs}
// A typed value rather than a slider: the length is a setting to compare a
// few chosen values of, not something to scrub through. The field turns red
// while its text isn't a usable length.
viewof buffonLengthInput = {
  const view = Inputs.text({label: "Length ℓ (spacing t = 1)", value: String(VM.ui.urlParam("buffon_len", buffonDefaultLength)), placeholder: "Between 0 and 1, e.g. 0.8"})
  const input = view.querySelector("input")
  const check = () => input.classList.toggle("vm-invalid", buffonParseLength(input.value) === null)
  view.addEventListener("input", check)
  check()
  return view
}
```

</div>

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// buffonParseLength: the length a field's text names, or null when it isn't
// one -- empty, mid-typing, not positive, or longer than the line spacing,
// where the formula 2ℓ/(πt) stops holding.
function buffonParseLength(text) {
  const parsed = VM.expressions.makeNumber(window.math, text)
  if (parsed === null || !Number.isFinite(parsed) || parsed <= 0 || parsed > buffonSpacing) return null
  return parsed
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// buffonLength: the typed length, or the default while the field is invalid.
buffonLength = {
  const parsed = buffonParseLength(buffonLengthInput)
  if (parsed === null) return buffonDefaultLength
  return parsed
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
buffonSeed = {
  if (buffonRedraw === 0) return VM.ui.urlParam("buffon_seed", buffonDefaultSeed)
  return Math.floor(Math.random() * 1e9)
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// buffonDrops: each drop's center and direction, drawn once per seed. The
// length input and the needle/noodle switch only redraw the shape about
// those centers, so changing them shows the same drops.
buffonDrops = dropNeedles(VM.sampling.seededRandom(buffonSeed), buffonMaxN, buffonWidth, buffonHeight)
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// buffonNeedles: polylines and crossings for the current shape and length;
// crossingCount[i] and crossingSquares[i] sum the crossings and their
// squares over the first i drops.
buffonNeedles = needleCrossings(buffonDrops, buffonLength, buffonSpacing, buffonShape.toLowerCase())
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
buffonStats = buffonEstimate(buffonNeedles.crossingCount[buffonN], buffonNeedles.crossingSquares[buffonN], buffonN, buffonLength, buffonSpacing)
```

```{ojs}
    {label: "|estimate − π|", value: format(buffonStats.error)}

}
```

```{ojs}
{
  // Drops as one trace per color, polylines separated by nulls -- a
  // single trace draws thousands of segments far faster than one trace each.
  const crossX = [], crossY = [], otherX = [], otherY = []
  for (let i = 0; i < buffonN; i++) {
    let xs = otherX, ys = otherY
    if (buffonNeedles.crossings[i] > 0) {
      xs = crossX
      ys = crossY
    }
    xs.push(...buffonNeedles.xs[i], null)
    ys.push(...buffonNeedles.ys[i], null)
  }

  const lineX = [], lineY = []
  for (let k = 0; k * buffonSpacing <= buffonHeight; k++) {
    lineX.push(-0.5, buffonWidth + 0.5, null)
    lineY.push(k * buffonSpacing, k * buffonSpacing, null)
  }

  const data = []
  if (buffonShow.has("Lines")) {
    data.push({x: lineX, y: lineY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Lines", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.muted, width: 1.5}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (buffonShow.has("Not crossing")) {
    data.push({x: otherX, y: otherY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Not crossing", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.fn, width: 2}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (buffonShow.has("Crossing a line")) {
    data.push({x: crossX, y: crossY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Crossing a line", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.alt, width: 2}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }

  return buffonPlot(data, {
    xaxis: {range: [-0.5, buffonWidth + 0.5], zeroline: false, showgrid: false, showticklabels: false, ticks: "", constrain: "domain"},
    yaxis: {range: [-0.6, buffonHeight + 0.6], zeroline: false, showgrid: false, showticklabels: false, ticks: "", scaleanchor: "x", constrain: "domain"},
    hovermode: false,
    uirevision: "static",
    autosize: true
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
buffonRunsPlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "400px"})
buffonErrorPlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "400px"})

// The app's length, once typing has paused: each redraw simulates 200 runs of
// 10,000 needles, too much for every keystroke. Text that isn't a usable length
// leaves the charts as they are.
buffonPlotLength = Generators.observe(notify => {
  const input = viewof buffonLengthInput
  let timer = null
  const onInput = () => {
    clearTimeout(timer)
    timer = setTimeout(() => {
      const parsed = buffonParseLength(input.value)
      if (parsed !== null) notify(parsed)
    }, 300)
  }
  const initial = buffonParseLength(input.value)
  if (initial === null) notify(buffonDefaultLength)
  else notify(initial)
  input.addEventListener("input", onInput)
  return () => {
    clearTimeout(timer)
    input.removeEventListener("input", onInput)
  }
})

// Fixed seeds, so the same length always draws the same picture.
buffonRuns = runningBuffonEstimates(VM.sampling.seededRandom(44), piRunCounts, 8, buffonPlotLength, buffonSpacing)
buffonErrors = randomBuffonErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(45), checkpoints(10000), 200, buffonPlotLength, buffonSpacing)
```

```{ojs}
  })

  const figure = document.createElement("div")
  figure.append(chart, piLegendKey([
    {label: "Independent runs", color: VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.6)},
    {label: "π", color: chartColors.alt, dashed: true}
  ]))
  return figure
}
```

### How often does a needle cross?

Describe a drop by two numbers: the angle $\theta \in [0, \pi)$ the needle makes with the lines, and the distance $d$ from its center to the nearest line. The center lands uniformly between two lines and the angle is uniform, independently of the center.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// The diagram's fixed sizes: spacing t = 1, and a needle long enough to read.
// The dot starts on a drop that misses, so the gap between d and h shows.
buffonFigLength = 0.84
buffonFigStart = ({theta: 50 * Math.PI / 180, d: 0.42})
buffonFigThetaRange = [-0.1, Math.PI + 0.1]
buffonFigDRange = [-0.02, 0.52]
buffonFigNeedlePlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "420px"})
buffonFigRegionPlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "420px"})
// The axes are fixed, so the zoom and pan toolbar would do nothing here.
buffonFigConfig = ({...VM.plotting.config(), displayModeBar: false})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const theta = buffonFigDrop.theta
  const d = buffonFigDrop.d
  const half = buffonFigLength / 2
  const h = half * Math.sin(theta)
  const tipX = -half * Math.cos(theta)
  const tipY = d - h
  const upperX = -tipX
  const upperY = d + h
  // Which way the lower tip leans: 1 for left, -1 for right. Labels go on the
  // side that keeps them clear of the needle.
  let side = 1
  if (tipX > 0) side = -1

  // The arc marking the angle between the needle and the level of its center.
  const arcX = [], arcY = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 30; k++) {
    const angle = Math.PI + theta * k / 30
    arcX.push(0.11 * Math.cos(angle))
    arcY.push(d + 0.11 * Math.sin(angle))
  }

  const segment = (x, y, color, width, dash) => ({
    x, y, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip",
    line: {color, width, dash}
  })
  const data = [
    // Where the center can be: every point within t/2 of the bold line.
    {x: [-0.95, 0.95, 0.95, -0.95, -0.95], y: [-0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5], type: "scatter", mode: "lines", fill: "toself",
      fillcolor: VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.muted, 0.12), showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip", line: {width: 0}},
    // Three lines, with the one nearest the center in bold.
    segment([-0.95, 0.95], [-1, -1], chartColors.muted, 1.5, "solid"),
    segment([-0.95, 0.95], [1, 1], chartColors.muted, 1.5, "solid"),
    segment([-0.95, 0.95], [0, 0], chartColors.ink, 2.5, "solid"),
    segment([0.8, 0.8], [0, 1], chartColors.muted, 1, "dot"),
    segment([Math.min(tipX, -0.2), Math.max(tipX, 0.2)], [d, d], chartColors.ink, 1, "dot"),
    segment([tipX, tipX], [tipY, d], chartColors.warn, 2.5, "dash"),
    segment([0, 0], [0, d], chartColors.alt, 2.5, "solid"),
    segment(arcX, arcY, chartColors.ink, 1.5, "solid"),
    segment([tipX, upperX], [tipY, upperY], chartColors.fn, 5, "solid"),
    {x: [0], y: [d], type: "scatter", mode: "markers", showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip",
      marker: {color: chartColors.fn, size: 10}}
  ]

  const label = (x, y, text, color) => ({x, y, text, showarrow: false, font: {color, size: 15}})
  const thetaLabelAngle = Math.PI + theta / 2
  return buffonFigNeedlePlot(data, {
    title: {text: "One drop"}, margin: {t: 40, l: 10, r: 10, b: 10},
    xaxis: {range: [-1, 1], visible: false, fixedrange: true, constrain: "domain"},
    yaxis: {range: [-1.05, 1.05], visible: false, fixedrange: true, scaleanchor: "x", constrain: "domain"},
    annotations: [
      label(side * 0.05, d / 2, "d", chartColors.alt),
      label(tipX - side * 0.05, (tipY + d) / 2, "h", chartColors.warn),
      label(0.18 * Math.cos(thetaLabelAngle), d + 0.18 * Math.sin(thetaLabelAngle), "θ", chartColors.ink),
      label(upperX / 2 + side * 0.09 * Math.sin(theta), (d + upperY) / 2 - 0.09 * Math.abs(Math.cos(theta)), "ℓ/2", chartColors.fn),
      label(0.85, 0.5, "t", chartColors.muted)
    ],
    hovermode: false, uirevision: "static", autosize: true
  }, buffonFigConfig)
}
```

```{ojs}
// buffonFigDrop: the dragged point (theta, d). The chart itself is the input,
// and the cell below paints it, so changing the theme keeps the dot in place.
viewof buffonFigDrop = {
  const div = buffonFigRegionPlot([], {}, buffonFigConfig)
  div.value = buffonFigStart
  // Without this a touch on the chart would scroll the page instead of moving the dot.
  div.style.touchAction = "none"

  const clamp = (value, low, high) => Math.min(high, Math.max(low, value))
  const moveTo = event => {
    // Plotly's drag layer covers exactly the plotting area, so pixels map
    // linearly onto the fixed axis ranges.
    const area = div.querySelector(".nsewdrag").getBoundingClientRect()
    const fractionX = (event.clientX - area.left) / area.width
    const fractionY = (area.bottom - event.clientY) / area.height
    const theta = buffonFigThetaRange[0] + fractionX * (buffonFigThetaRange[1] - buffonFigThetaRange[0])
    const d = buffonFigDRange[0] + fractionY * (buffonFigDRange[1] - buffonFigDRange[0])
    div.value = {theta: clamp(theta, 0, Math.PI), d: clamp(d, 0, 0.5)}
    div.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}))
  }

  let dragging = false
  div.addEventListener("pointerdown", event => {
    dragging = true
    div.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId)
    moveTo(event)
  })
  div.addEventListener("pointermove", event => {
    if (dragging) moveTo(event)
  })
  div.addEventListener("pointerup", () => { dragging = false })
  div.addEventListener("pointercancel", () => { dragging = false })
  return div
}
```

### The estimator

If $C$ of $N$ needles cross a line, then $C/N \approx P(\text{cross})$. Solving for $\pi$ gives the estimator


$$
\hat{\pi}_N = \frac{2 \ell N}{t\, C}.
$$

::: {.callout-important}
## A ratio estimator
Unlike $\hat\pi_N$ from the circle, which averages $N$ independent draws, this estimator *divides* by a random count. It is undefined until the first crossing, biased upward for every finite $N$, and noisier than the circle's estimate, more so the shorter the needle. You work out by how much in @sec-buffon-ratio.
:::

By linearity of expectation, the shape of the needle doesn't matter, only its length. Try changing the shape in the app above: the estimate still converges to $\pi$. Linearity, however, is a property of expectation alone. The variance, and with it the bias, does depend on the shape, and for $\ell \le t$ the straight needle has the lowest variance possible.

### Bias, variance and MSE of a ratio {#sec-buffon-ratio}

Write $p = P(\text{cross})$ and $\hat p = C/N$ for the fraction of needles that cross, so that

$$
\hat\pi_N = \frac{2\ell}{t}\cdot\frac{1}{\hat p} = \pi\cdot\frac{p}{\hat p}.
$$

Here $\hat p$ is an ordinary Monte Carlo average. The trouble is that the estimator inverts it, and $1/x$ is not linear, so the circle's calculations don't carry over.

:::: {.callout-note}
## Exercises: An Undefined Estimator

::: {#exr-buffon-zero}
What is the distribution of $C$? Find the mean and variance of $\hat p$.

- Find $P(C = 0)$ and the value of $\hat\pi_N$ on that event. What does this say about $\mathbb{E}[\hat\pi_N]$?
- Evaluate $P(C = 0)$ for $\ell = t = 1$ and $N = 100$.
:::

::::

Since $C = 0$ is so rare, what one means by the bias of $\hat\pi_N$ is its mean given $C \ge 1$, minus $\pi$. A Taylor expansion approximates it.

:::: {.callout-note}
## Exercises: Bias

::: {#exr-buffon-bias}
Expand $1/\hat p$ to second order about $p$ and take expectations to approximate $\mathbb{E}[\hat\pi_N]$ and the bias of $\hat\pi_N$, in terms of $p$ and $N$. How fast does the bias shrink with $N$?
:::

::: {#exr-buffon-jensen}
Use Jensen's inequality to explain the sign of the bias. Is $t\hat p/(2\ell)$, the matching estimate of $1/\pi$, biased?
:::

::::

For the variance, one term of the expansion is enough. The *delta method* approximates a smooth function $g$ of an estimator by its linear Taylor term about $p$, which gives

$$
\text{Var}(g(\hat p)) \approx g'(p)^2\, \text{Var}(\hat p).
$$

:::: {.callout-note}
## Exercises: Variance

::: {#exr-buffon-variance}
Apply the delta method with $g(x) = \frac{2\ell}{t}\cdot\frac{1}{x}$ to approximate $\text{Var}(\hat\pi_N)$ and $\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$, in terms of $p$ and $N$.
:::

::: {#exr-buffon-readout}
With the shape set to *Needle*, the app's *Standard error* readout is $\frac{2\ell}{t}\sqrt{\frac{1 - \hat p}{N \hat p^3}}$.

- Show that this is your formula with $\hat p$ in place of $p$.
- Set $\ell = 1$ and $N = 1000$, and compare the readout with your formula.
:::

::: {#exr-buffon-length}
How does $\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$ grow as $\ell \to 0$?

- Predict the ratio of the standard errors at $\ell = 0.25$ and $\ell = 1$, then check it with the readout at $N = 2000$.
- Take the longest needle, $\ell = t$. How many needles does it take to match the accuracy of $N$ random points in the circle method (@exr-pi-variance)?
:::

::::

The *mean squared error* $\text{MSE}(\hat\pi_N) = \mathbb{E}[(\hat\pi_N - \pi)^2]$ combines the two kinds of error.

:::: {.callout-note}

## Non-random methods for estimating $\pi$

Both methods above converge at the Monte Carlo rate $O(N^{-1/2})$: each extra decimal digit costs a hundred times more samples. Dropping the randomness does better. This section counts points on a grid instead, then fills the square with points that are spread out on purpose, which sit in between the two.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
gaussMaxR = 40
gaussDefaultR = 8
gaussTraceOptions = ["Inside", "Outside", "Circle"]
gaussTraceColors = new Map([
  ["Inside", chartColors.fn],
  ["Outside", chartColors.muted],
  ["Circle", chartColors.ink]
])

haltonMaxN = 10000
haltonDefaultN = 1000
haltonTraceOptions = ["Inside", "Outside", "Circle and square"]
haltonTraceColors = new Map([
  ["Inside", chartColors.fn],
  ["Outside", chartColors.warn],
  ["Circle and square", chartColors.ink]
])

// The circle x² + y² = r², for drawing only.
function circlePath(r) {
  const xs = [], ys = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 200; k++) {
    xs.push(r * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * k / 200))
    ys.push(r * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * k / 200))
  }
  return {xs, ys}
}
```

### The Gauss circle method

Count the integer points $(x, y)$ with $x^2 + y^2 \le r^2$. Each counted point is the center of a unit square, and together those squares cover the disk of radius $r$ up to a ragged edge, so the count $L(r)$ is about the disk's area $\pi r^2$ and

$$
\hat\pi_r = \frac{L(r)}{r^2} \to \pi.
$$

Gauss bounded the error: every square that sticks out of the disk, or every piece of the disk no square covers, lies within $\sqrt 2/2$ of the circle, so $|L(r) - \pi r^2| \le 2\sqrt2\,\pi r + 2\pi$ and $|\hat\pi_r - \pi| = O(1/r)$. How fast that is depends on what you count. Per grid point, it is not much faster than Monte Carlo. Against the $N = (2r+1)^2$ points of the square, $O(1/r)$ is $O(N^{-1/2})$, the Monte Carlo rate, though now a guaranteed bound rather than a standard error. The true error is smaller, because the errors along the edge mostly cancel. Finding how small $L(r) - \pi r^2$ really is, is the *Gauss circle problem*: it is known to be $O(r^{0.63})$ and conjectured to be $O(r^{1/2 + \varepsilon})$, which would make the error of $\hat\pi_r$ about $O(N^{-3/4})$.

The real gain is that nobody has to look at every point. Column $x$ of the disk holds exactly $2\lfloor\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\rfloor + 1$ points, so $L(r)$ takes $2r + 1$ integer square roots. Measured against that work, $W \approx 2r$, the error is $O(W^{-1})$ for certain and about $O(W^{-3/2})$ by the conjecture, against $W^{-1/2}$ for any random method. Ten times the work gives one more digit at least, instead of a hundred times the work.

### Halton points: in between

The grid is rigid: to refine it you must start over with a finer one, and its points line up in rows that meet the circle all at once. Random points can be added one at a time, but they clump and leave gaps, and that unevenness is where the $N^{-1/2}$ comes from. A *low-discrepancy* sequence has the best of both: it can be extended one point at a time, like random sampling, but each new point goes where the earlier ones left the biggest gap, so the first $N$ points always cover the square evenly.

The Halton sequence builds one from the van der Corput sequence: write $i$ in base $b$ and mirror its digits about the radix point, so in base 2, $1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots = 1_2, 10_2, 11_2, 100_2, \ldots$ become $0.1_2, 0.01_2, 0.11_2, 0.001_2, \ldots = \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac34, \tfrac18, \ldots$, each point halving a gap left by the last. The $i$-th Halton point uses base 2 for $x$ and base 3 for $y$, mapped from $[0,1]^2$ to $[-1,1]^2$. Feeding these points to the circle method's estimator $4 \cdot (\text{inside})/N$ is *quasi-Monte Carlo*. For smooth integrands its error is $O((\log N)^2/N)$ (the Koksma–Hlawka inequality); the disk's sharp edge costs some of that, and here the error falls roughly like $N^{-3/4}$. At $N = 10{,}000$ it is typically a tenth of the random method's standard error. Compare the two apps at the same $N$.

```{ojs}
  {label: "Estimate of π", value: haltonStats.estimate.toFixed(4), title: "4 · inside / N"},
  {label: "|estimate − π|", value: haltonStats.error.toFixed(4)},
  {label: "Random SE at this N", value: Math.sqrt(Math.PI * (4 - Math.PI) / haltonN).toFixed(4),
    title: "sqrt(π(4 − π) / N), the circle method's standard error, for comparison"}
])
```

### The three side by side

The figure plots each circle method's error against the number of points it uses, on log-log axes, where a rate $N^{-a}$ is a straight line of slope $-a$. Random points give the RMS error over 40 runs, with a band holding the middle 80% of runs. The Gauss circle method's points are the $(2r+1)^2$ grid points of the square, for every radius $r$; counted by work instead, its curve would shift left to $N \approx 2r$ and fall faster than every other one.

```{ojs}
//| output: false
cmpMaxN = 1e5
cmpCounts = checkpoints(cmpMaxN)
cmpSeries = [
  {label: "Random points", token: "fn", points: randomCircleErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(7), cmpCounts, 40), scatter: false},
  {label: "Gauss circle", token: "warn", points: latticeErrors(cmpMaxN), scatter: true},
  {label: "Halton points", token: "ok", points: haltonCircleErrors(checkpoints(cmpMaxN, 24)), scatter: true}
]
cmpPlot = VM.plotting.persistentPlot({height: "480px"})
```

::: {#fig-pi-methods}

```{ojs}
{
  const data = []
  for (const s of cmpSeries) {
    const color = chartColors[s.token]
    const xs = [], ys = [], lo = [], hi = []
    for (const p of s.points) {
      xs.push(p.n)
      ys.push(p.error)
      if (p.lo !== undefined) {
        lo.push(Math.max(p.lo, 1e-9))
        hi.push(p.hi)
      }
    }
    // The curve comes first: VM.plotting.plotWithLegend colors a legend row
    // after the first trace of that name.
    let mode = "lines+markers"
    let size = 5
    if (s.scatter) {
      mode = "markers"
      size = 3
    }
    data.push({
      type: "scatter", mode, name: s.label,
      x: xs, y: ys, line: {color, width: 2}, marker: {color, size},
      hovertemplate: `<b>${s.label}</b><br>N = %{x}<br>error = %{y:.2e}<extra></extra>`
    })
    if (s.scatter) {
      // The deterministic errors swing from one N to the next, crossing zero
      // now and then, so their points stay unjoined and their rate is drawn
      // as the fitted line instead. Same name as the markers, so the legend
      // row hides the line too.
      // Solid over the fitted range N ≥ 100, dashed where it is extended
      // back to the first point.
      const fit = convergenceFit(s.points)
      const fitLine = n => 10 ** fit.intercept * n ** -fit.order
      const first = xs[0]
      const last = xs[xs.length - 1]
      data.push({type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: s.label, hoverinfo: "skip",
        x: [100, last], y: [fitLine(100), fitLine(last)], line: {color, width: 2}})
      data.push({type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: s.label, hoverinfo: "skip",
        x: [first, 100], y: [fitLine(first), fitLine(100)], line: {color, width: 2, dash: "dash"}})
    }
    if (lo.length > 0) {
      // The 10%-90% band: the upper edge, then the lower edge filled up to
      // it. Same name as the curve, so its legend row hides the band too.
      data.push({type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: s.label, hoverinfo: "skip",
        x: xs, y: hi, line: {width: 0, color}})
      data.push({type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: s.label, hoverinfo: "skip",
        x: xs, y: lo, line: {width: 0, color}, fill: "tonexty", fillcolor: VM.plotting.alpha(s.token, 0.15)})
    }
  }
  // Reference slopes, unnamed so the legend leaves them on.
  data.push({type: "scatter", mode: "lines", showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip",
    x: [10, cmpMaxN], y: [1, Math.sqrt(10 / cmpMaxN)], line: {color: chartColors.muted, width: 1, dash: "dash"}})
  data.push({type: "scatter", mode: "lines", showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip",
    x: [10, cmpMaxN], y: [0.3, 0.3 * 10 / cmpMaxN], line: {color: chartColors.muted, width: 1, dash: "dot"}})
  return VM.plotting.plotWithLegend(cmpPlot, data, {
    xaxis: {type: "log", title: "N (points used)"},
    yaxis: {type: "log", title: "|estimate − π|", exponentformat: "power"},
    annotations: [
      {x: Math.log10(cmpMaxN), y: Math.log10(Math.sqrt(10 / cmpMaxN)), text: "N⁻¹ᐟ²", showarrow: false, xanchor: "left"},
      {x: Math.log10(cmpMaxN), y: Math.log10(0.3 * 10 / cmpMaxN), text: "N⁻¹", showarrow: false, xanchor: "left"}
    ],
    hovermode: "closest", uirevision: "static", autosize: true
  })
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const stats = []
  for (const s of cmpSeries) {
    stats.push({label: s.label, value: `order ≈ ${convergenceOrder(s.points).toFixed(2)}`,
      title: "minus the slope of the least-squares line through the log-log points with N ≥ 100"})
  }
  return VM.ui.statRow(stats)
}
```

Error of the three points-in-a-circle estimates of π against the number of points N. The two deterministic errors swing widely from one N to the next, dipping wherever the estimate crosses π, so they are shown as points (Gauss: one per radius; Halton: 24 per decade) with their least-squares lines, fitted over N ≥ 100 and extended (dashed) below it. Dashed and dotted lines: the rates N⁻¹ᐟ² and N⁻¹.

### For fun: $\pi$ from other numerical methods

The methods on this page against some deterministic ones. Several apps on [VisualMathLab](https://www.visualmathlab.com) compute $\pi$ when given the right inputs; each link opens that app on its own with those inputs filled in. The rows run from slowest to fastest. To make them comparable, the error column measures every method by its work $N$: samples drawn, grid columns counted (the Gauss circle method counts each of its $2r+1$ columns in one step), or function evaluations (Newton's method evaluates sin and cos at each step, three digits gained per step, so its error after $N$ evaluations is about $e^{-c\,3^{N/2}}$; iterating $x + \sin x$ needs only sin). The random methods' rates are standard errors, Halton's is the fitted rate from the figure above, and the rest are worst-case bounds.

| Method | π is | Error | App |
|---|---|---|---|
| Circle method (random points) | 4 × P(a uniform point of the square lands in the disk) | $O(N^{-1/2})$ | [above](#pi-app) |
| Buffon's needle / Barbier's noodle | 2ℓ / (t × mean crossings per drop) | $O(N^{-1/2})$ | [above](#buffon-app) |
| Circle method (Halton points) | 4 × fraction of Halton points in the disk | about $O(N^{-3/4})$ | [above](#halton-app) |
| Gauss circle method | lattice points in the disk of radius r, divided by r² | $O(N^{-1})$ proven, about $O(N^{-3/2})$ conjectured | [above](#gauss-app) |
| Linear interpolation | the length of y = √(1 − x²) over [−1, 1], a semicircle | $O(N^{-3/2})$ | [Linear interpolation of the semicircle](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/polynomial-interpolation/index.html?embed=1&f=sqrt(1-x%5E2)&a=-1&b=1&max=40&n=8&show=original,linear,nodes){target="_blank"} |
| Cubic spline | the length of y = √(1 − x²) over [−1, 1] | $O(N^{-3/2})$ | [Cubic spline of the semicircle](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/polynomial-interpolation/index.html?embed=1&f=sqrt(1-x%5E2)&a=-1&b=1&max=40&n=8&show=original,cubic,nodes){target="_blank"} |
| Adaptive Simpson | ∫₀¹ 4/(1 + x²) dx | $O(N^{-6})$ | [Adaptive integration of 4/(1 + x²)](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/adaptive-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=4%2F(1%2Bx%5E2)&a=0&b=1){target="_blank"} |
| Adaptive Simpson | ∫₀¹ 4√(1 − x²) dx, four quarter disks | $O(N^{-6})$ | [Adaptive integration of 4√(1 − x²)](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/adaptive-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=4*sqrt(1-x%5E2)&a=0&b=1){target="_blank"} |
| Adaptive Simpson | (∫₋₆⁶ e^−x²^ dx)² | $O(N^{-6})$ | [Adaptive integration of e^−x²^](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/adaptive-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=exp(-x%5E2)&a=-6&b=6){target="_blank"} |
| Trapezoid rule | (∫₋₆⁶ e^−x²^ dx)² | $O(e^{-cN^2})$ | [Trapezoid on e^−x²^](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/numerical-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=exp(-x%5E2)&a=-6&b=6&max=40&n=12&show=f,trapezoidal){target="_blank"} |
| Newton's method | the root of sin x, starting from 1.98 | $O(e^{-c\,3^{N/2}})$ | [Newton on sin x](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/newton-method/index.html?embed=1&f=sin(x)&x0=1.98&max=12){target="_blank"} |
| Fixed-point iteration | the fixed point of x + sin x, starting from 0.1 | $O(e^{-c\,3^N})$ | [Iterating x + sin x](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/fixed-point-iteration/index.html?embed=1&g=x%2Bsin(x)&x0=0.1&max=12){target="_blank"} |

Newton's method gains three digits per step, and the trapezoid rule on $e^{-x^2}$ reaches full double precision in about 22 evaluations; the circle method would need around $10^{30}$ samples for the same accuracy.
